title: Getting started: compiler & first programs
overview: Before writing any real C, you need a working toolchain: a C compiler (GCC from MinGW on Windows), an editor (VS Code) and a quick way to run a file (the Code Runner extension). This page sums up that setup and the two tiny programs used to check that everything works: one that only prints, and one that reads a number.

concepts.explain: C source code is plain text. A compiler (here `gcc`) turns it into an `.exe` the computer can run. You compile first, then run.
Windows only finds `gcc` from any folder if the compiler's `bin` folder is added to the `Path` system variable. Check it by opening a terminal and typing `gcc -v`; a version message means it worked.
Code Runner adds a Run button that saves the file, compiles it and runs it in one click. Its `executorMap` setting (in `settings.json`) holds the exact compile-and-run command for each language.
Set `code-runner.runInTerminal` to `true`. The Output panel is read-only, so a program that calls `scanf` can only receive your typing inside the terminal.
If your local setup is broken, an online compiler such as OnlineGDB lets you keep practising while you fix it.
A print-only program proves that compiling and running work. A program that reads input proves that typing into the terminal works too.

files.title: Hello World
files.what: The smallest useful C program: it prints one line. If this runs, your compiler and editor are set up correctly.
steps: `main` is where the program starts running.
`printf("Hello World!\n")` prints the text; `\n` moves to a new line.
`return 0;` tells the operating system the program finished without errors.
files.output_note: You should see exactly `Hello World!` on one line.
files.watch_out: If the terminal says `gcc` is not recognized, the MinGW `bin` folder is not in your `Path` yet.

check.q: What does `return 0;` at the end of `main` mean?
check.a: The program finished successfully. A non-zero value would signal an error.

files.title: Read one number and print it
files.what: Reads one integer with `scanf` and prints it back. It checks that keyboard input reaches your program.
steps: Declare `int a;` to hold the number.
`scanf("%d", &a)` waits for you to type an integer. `&a` gives `scanf` the address where it should store the value.
`printf("a = %d", a)` replaces `%d` with the value of `a`.
files.output_note: With input `42` the program prints `a = 42`. There is no `\n` at the end, so your terminal prompt may appear on the same line.
files.watch_out: If the program seems stuck, it is waiting for input. Type a number and press Enter. With Code Runner this only works when `runInTerminal` is on.

check.q: Why do we write `&a` in `scanf` but just `a` in `printf`?
check.a: `scanf` must change `a`, so it needs the variable's address. `printf` only needs its value.

recap: The workflow is always the same: write, compile with `gcc`, then run the `.exe`.
Add MinGW's `bin` folder to `Path`, then check with `gcc -v`.
In VS Code, Code Runner plus `runInTerminal: true` lets you run programs that read input.
`printf` writes output and `scanf` reads input. Both come from `<stdio.h>`.
Get Hello World running first, then test input.

check_yourself.q: You typed `gcc -v` and got 'command not found'. What is the most likely cause?
check_yourself.a: The compiler's `bin` folder is not in the `Path` environment variable, or you did not open a new terminal after adding it.

check_yourself.q: Why can't a program that uses `scanf` read your typing in VS Code's Output panel?
check_yourself.a: The Output panel only shows text; it cannot send keyboard input. Run the program in the integrated terminal instead.

check_yourself.q: What two steps happen when you press Run on a `.c` file?
check_yourself.a: The file is compiled into an executable, and then that executable is run.
